The **mayor of London** is the [strategic authority mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_authority_mayor "Strategic authority mayor") for the [Greater London Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London_Authority "Greater London Authority"). The role was created in 2000 after the [Greater London devolution referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Greater_London_Authority_referendum "1998 Greater London Authority referendum") in 1998, and was the first [directly elected mayor in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directly_elected_mayors_in_England "Directly elected mayors in England").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-2)
[Sadiq Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadiq_Khan "Sadiq Khan") took office as mayor on 9 May 2016, and was re-elected in 2021 and 2024. The position had been held by [Ken Livingstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Livingstone "Ken Livingstone") from the creation of the role on 4 May 2000 until he was defeated after two terms in May 2008 by [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson"), who also served two terms before Khan was elected.
The mayor is scrutinised by the [London Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Assembly "London Assembly") and, supported by their [Mayoral Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Mayor_of_London "Deputy Mayor of London"), is responsible for the strategic government of the entirety of London, including the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London") (for which there is also the [Lord Mayor of the City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayor_of_London "Lord Mayor of London")). Each of the 32 [London Boroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_boroughs "London boroughs") also has a ceremonial mayor or, [in Croydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Croydon "Mayor of Croydon"), [Hackney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Hackney "Mayor of Hackney"), [Lewisham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Lewisham "Mayor of Lewisham"), [Newham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Newham "Mayor of Newham") and [Tower Hamlets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Tower_Hamlets "Mayor of Tower Hamlets"), an elected mayor. The mayor of London is elected by the largest single-member electorate in the United Kingdom.
## Background
The [Greater London Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London_Council "Greater London Council"), the elected government for [Greater London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London "Greater London"), was abolished in 1986 by the [Local Government Act 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Government_Act_1985 "Local Government Act 1985"). Strategic functions were split off to various joint arrangements. Londoners voted in [a referendum in 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Greater_London_Authority_referendum "1998 Greater London Authority referendum") to create a new governance structure for Greater London. The directly elected mayor of London was created by the [Greater London Authority Act 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London_Authority_Act_1999 "Greater London Authority Act 1999") in 2000 as part of the reforms.
## Elections
Main article: [London mayoral elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_mayoral_elections "London mayoral elections")
The mayor is elected for a fixed term of four years, with elections taking place in May. 
Voting is conducted by the [supplementary vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplementary_vote "Supplementary vote") method, except in 2024 when the [first-past-the-post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post_voting "First-past-the-post voting") system was substituted by the [Elections Act 2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_Act_2022 "Elections Act 2022"), which was passed by the [Conservative government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Boris_Johnson "Premiership of Boris Johnson"). In 2026, the [Labour government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Keir_Starmer "Premiership of Keir Starmer") restored the supplementary vote.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-3)
There are no limits on the number of terms a mayor may serve. The mayor is elected by the largest single-member electorate in the United Kingdom.
As with most elected posts in the United Kingdom, there is a deposit (in this case of £10,000), which is returnable on the candidate's winning of at least 5% of votes cast.
### 2024 election
Main article: [2024 London mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_London_mayoral_election "2024 London mayoral election")
A London mayoral election was held on 2 May 2024,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-4) with results announced on 4 May.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-5) Sadiq Khan was re-elected as mayor beating the Conservative [Susan Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Hall "Susan Hall"), becoming the first mayor elected for three terms.

## Powers and functions
Most powers are derived from the [Greater London Authority Act 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London_Authority_Act_1999 "Greater London Authority Act 1999"), with additional functions coming from the [Greater London Authority Act 2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London_Authority_Act_2007 "Greater London Authority Act 2007"), the [Localism Act 2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Localism_Act_2011 "Localism Act 2011") and [Police Reform and Social Responsibility Act 2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_Reform_and_Social_Responsibility_Act_2011 "Police Reform and Social Responsibility Act 2011").
The mayor's main functions are:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-12)
  * Strategic planning, including housing, waste management, the environment and production of the [London Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Plan "London Plan")
  * Refuse or permit planning permission on strategic grounds
  * Transport policy, delivered by functional body [Transport for London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_for_London "Transport for London")
  * Fire and emergency planning, delivered by functional body [London Fire and Emergency Planning Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Fire_and_Emergency_Planning_Authority "London Fire and Emergency Planning Authority")
  * Policing and crime policy, delivered by functional body [Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor's_Office_for_Policing_and_Crime "Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime") (before 2012 by functional body [Metropolitan Police Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police_Authority "Metropolitan Police Authority")). The [Metropolitan Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police "Metropolitan Police") has a structure different to most others across the country, reporting to the Mayor of London instead of a [police and crime commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_and_crime_commissioner "Police and crime commissioner").
  * Economic development, delivered directly by the Greater London Authority through subsidiary company [GLA Land and Property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLA_Land_and_Property "GLA Land and Property") (before 2012 by functional body [London Development Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Development_Agency "London Development Agency"))
  * Power to create development corporations, such as the [London Legacy Development Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Legacy_Development_Corporation "London Legacy Development Corporation")


The remaining local government functions are performed by the [London borough councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_borough_council "London borough council"). There is some overlap; for example, the borough councils are responsible for waste management, but the mayor is required to produce a waste management strategy.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-13) In 2010, Johnson launched an initiative in partnership with the Multi-academy Trust [AET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academies_Enterprise_Trust "Academies Enterprise Trust") to transform schools across London. This led to the establishment of [London Academies Enterprise Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Academies_Enterprise_Trust "London Academies Enterprise Trust") ([LAET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Academies_Enterprise_Trust "London Academies Enterprise Trust")) which was intended to be a group of ten academies, but it only reached a group of four before the mayor withdrew it in 2013. The mayor is a member of the [Mayoral Council for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayoral_Council_for_England "Mayoral Council for England") and the [Council of the Nations and Regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_the_Nations_and_Regions "Council of the Nations and Regions").

## Initiatives
### Ken Livingstone
Initiatives taken by [Ken Livingstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Livingstone "Ken Livingstone") as Mayor of London included the [London congestion charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_congestion_charge "London congestion charge") on private vehicles using city centre London on weekdays, the creation of the [London Climate Change Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C40_Cities_Climate_Leadership_Group "C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group"), the London Energy Partnership and the founding of the international [Large Cities Climate Leadership Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_Cities_Climate_Leadership_Group "Large Cities Climate Leadership Group"), now known as [C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C40_Cities_Climate_Leadership_Group "C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group"). The congestion charge led to many new buses being introduced across London. In August 2003, Livingstone oversaw the introduction of the [Oyster card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyster_card "Oyster card") electronic ticketing system for [Transport for London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_for_London "Transport for London") services.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-cw-20030819-15) Livingstone supported the withdrawal of the vintage [AEC Routemaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEC_Routemaster "AEC Routemaster") buses from regular service in London.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-16)
Livingstone introduced the London Partnerships Register which was a voluntary scheme without legal force for same sex couples to register their partnership, and paved the way for the introduction by the United Kingdom Parliament of [civil partnerships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_partnership "Civil partnership") and later still, [Same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage"). Unlike civil partnerships, the London Partnerships Register was open to heterosexual couples who favour a public commitment other than marriage.
As Mayor of London, Livingstone was a supporter of the [London Olympics in 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics"), ultimately winning the bid to host the Games in 2005. Livingstone encouraged sport in London; especially when sport could be combined with helping charities like The London Marathon and 10K charity races. Livingstone, in a mayoral election debate on the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC")'s _[Question Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Question_Time_\(TV_programme\) "Question Time \(TV programme\)")_ in April 2008, stated that the primary reason he supported the Olympic bid was to secure funding for the redevelopment of the [East End of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_End_of_London "East End of London"). In July 2007, he brought the [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Tour_de_France "2007 Tour de France") cycle race to London.
### Boris Johnson
In May 2008, [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") introduced a new transport safety initiative to put 440 high visibility police officers in and around bus stations.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-17) A ban on alcohol on underground, and Docklands Light Railway, tram services and stations across the capital was introduced.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-18)
Also in May 2008, he announced the closure of _The Londoner_ newspaper, saving approximately £2.9 million. A percentage of this saving was to be spent on planting 10,000 new street trees.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-19)
In 2010, he extended the coverage of [Oyster card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyster_card "Oyster card") electronic ticketing to all National Rail overground train services.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-20) Also in 2010, he opened [a cycle hire scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santander_Cycles "Santander Cycles") (originally sponsored by [Barclays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclays "Barclays") bank, now [Santander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santander_UK "Santander UK") bank) with 5,000 bicycles available for hire across London. Although initiated by his predecessor, [Ken Livingstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Livingstone "Ken Livingstone"), the scheme rapidly acquired the nickname of "Boris Bikes". Johnson withdrew the recently introduced high-speed high-capacity "[bendy buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articulated_bus "Articulated bus")" which had been bought by Livingstone from service in 2011, and supported the development of the [New Routemaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Routemaster "New Routemaster") bus[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-21) which entered service the next year.
In 2011, Boris Johnson set up the Outer London Fund of £50 million designed to help improve local high streets.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-22) Areas in London were given the chance to submit proposals for two tranches of funding. Successful bids for Phase 1 included Enfield,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-23) Muswell Hill[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-24) and Bexley town centre.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-25) As of 2011[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mayor_of_London&action=edit)
In January 2013, he appointed journalist [Andrew Gilligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gilligan "Andrew Gilligan") as the first Cycling Commissioner for London.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-26) In March 2013, Johnson announced £1 billion of investment in infrastructure to make cycling safer in London, including a 15-mile (24 km) East to West segregated 'Crossrail for bikes'.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-27)
At the [general election of 7 May 2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"), Johnson was elected MP for [Uxbridge and South Ruislip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uxbridge_and_South_Ruislip_\(UK_Parliament_constituency\) "Uxbridge and South Ruislip \(UK Parliament constituency\)"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-28) He continued to serve as mayor for the remainder of his term, and was not a candidate in the mayoral election of May 2016, won by Labour's [Sadiq Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadiq_Khan "Sadiq Khan"). Johnson was later [elected prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Boris_Johnson "Premiership of Boris Johnson") in 2019.

## Controversies
### Ken Livingstone
In February 2006, Livingstone was suspended from office for four weeks by the [Adjudication Panel for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjudication_Panel_for_England "Adjudication Panel for England") after telling a Jewish reporter from the _[Evening Standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard "Evening Standard")_ , who had asked him for a comment outside a City Hall reception, that he was acting "just like a concentration camp guard." The panel found he had brought his office into disrepute.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-39) Livingstone appealed to the [High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Justice "High Court of Justice"), which quashed the suspension in October 2006; justice [Andrew Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Collins_\(judge\) "Andrew Collins \(judge\)") ruled the remark "unnecessarily offensive" and "indefensible" but found the panel had misdirected itself, as Livingstone had not been acting in an official capacity.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-40)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-41)
### Boris Johnson
Johnson strongly backed the [Garden Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_Bridge "Garden Bridge"), a proposed pedestrian crossing over the [Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") with extensive planting, from 2013. After he left office, Sadiq Khan commissioned an independent review led by Dame [Margaret Hodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Hodge "Margaret Hodge"), which raised concerns about value for money and recommended the scheme not proceed; Khan withdrew the mayoral guarantee and the project was abandoned in 2017. A subsequent [Transport for London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_for_London "Transport for London") report found the bridge had cost £53.5 million, almost £43 million of it public funds, with no reasonable prospect of recovery.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-42)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-43)
In 2014, Johnson authorised the purchase of three second-hand [water cannons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_cannons "Water cannons") from the German police for over £320,000, anticipating public disorder. In 2015, Home Secretary [Theresa May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_May "Theresa May") refused to license them for use in England and Wales on safety grounds; Khan's administration sold them for scrap in 2018 for just over £11,000, a net loss of more than £300,000.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-44)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-45)
### Sadiq Khan
In August 2023, Khan expanded the [Ultra Low Emission Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_Low_Emission_Zone "Ultra Low Emission Zone") (ULEZ) to cover all of Greater London, requiring non-compliant vehicles to pay a £12.50 daily charge. The expansion proved highly contentious, with critics, including several outer London councils and Conservative politicians, arguing that it imposed a disproportionate financial burden on drivers in outer London, particularly those on lower incomes, while supporters, such as health campaigners and medical organisations, pointed to the scheme's expected air quality and public health benefits.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-46)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-47)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-48) Several councils mounted an unsuccessful legal challenge against the expansion.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-49)
Following the [7 October 2023 Hamas attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_7_attacks "October 7 attacks"), large pro-Palestinian marches in central London prompted calls from some Conservative politicians and Jewish community leaders for Khan to curtail or ban the demonstrations.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-50)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-51) Khan said the right to peaceful protest was a "cornerstone" of democracy and that the Mayor lacked legal powers to ban marches, while condemning [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_in_the_United_Kingdom "Antisemitism in the United Kingdom") and extremist behaviour and urging protesters to be mindful of Jewish Londoners' fears.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-52)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London#cite_note-53)
